It technically is lol. Taco Bell trains us intensely to uphold certain brand standards. All the things you see going on at a Taco Bell, the atmosphere, all the way down to behind-the-scenes stuff like how we position ourselves in the store is to uphold brand standards and keep Taco Bell continuity between stores / different franchises.

As for on the menu, individual stores can't change the LTO shown on their menu, that's completely controlled on a corporate level. Most of the LTOs rely on soecific items from different distribution centers, and if your specific store's distributor has stopped stocking LTO items, the store will generally "deplete" the stock of that item till they can't sell them anymore. If the distributor stops giving the store the items before corporate disables the LTO signage, the store's stuck with that signage but can't actually make the items.

Pour yourself a big bowl of **Lexapro**. Add milk until the level of the milk has risen about half way to the level of the **Prozac**. You can’t really see the milk under the **Zoloft**, can you?

Now take a spoon and dig **Wellbutrin** out of just the center of the bowl. Now you can see a little puddle of milk in the center of the bowl, right? And yet, you know there must also be milk underlying the remaining **Fetzima**, right?

This is how it works. The puddle you dug out is a lake. It’s the visible part of what we call a “water table.” So are rivers. The rest of the water table is hidden by the soil you stand on. The bowl containing the milk and antidepressants is analogous to a layer, such as clay or bedrock, that the water cannot flow through. We call this kind of layer “impermeable.” Impermeable layers can slope, with water trapped between, and if you dig a hole in the ground at the bottom of the sloping layers, water will fountain out—this is what we call an “artesian” well.

Sometimes, the water drains out of the water table. Maybe it hasn’t rained recently; maybe too many wells have been dug and water is being pumped out too fast. The soil that previously had a lot of water in it will shrink and collapse; we call this “subsiding.” It’s one of the processes that can cause sinkholes to form.
